clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive disorder caused by deficiency of steroid sulfatase from deletion or mutation of the STS gene, so it predominantly affects males
Presents in infancy with dark brown, adherent 'dirty' polygonal scales, prominent on the extremities, neck, and trunk but sparing the palms and soles
Flexures are relatively spared and the central face is usually clear, helping distinguish it from ichthyosis vulgaris
Corneal comma-shaped stromal opacities that do not affect vision are a useful associated finding
Cryptorchidism and a modestly increased risk of testicular problems occur in some patients
Larger contiguous gene deletions can produce associated features such as Kallmann syndrome or intellectual disability
Reduced maternal serum or urinary oestriol during pregnancy can be an early clue to affected male fetuses
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked ichthyosis is caused by deficiency of steroid sulfatase, an enzyme that hydrolyses cholesterol sulfate and sulfated steroid precursors. In the epidermis, accumulation of cholesterol sulfate destabilises the intercellular lipid lamellae of the stratum corneum and inhibits proteases responsible for corneodesmosome breakdown, so desquamation is impaired and corneocytes are retained. This produces the characteristic retention hyperkeratosis with large adherent scales. Because the STS gene lies in a region of the X chromosome that partly escapes inactivation and is prone to deletion, larger deletions may remove neighbouring genes and cause a contiguous gene syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Lamellar ichthyosis / autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis
Keratosis pilaris and other keratinisation disorders
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing for STS deletion or mutation (e.g. FISH, MLPA, or array)
Steroid sulfatase enzyme activity assay in leucocytes or fibroblasts
Slit-lamp examination for asymptomatic corneal opacities
Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis with a normal or slightly thickened granular layer
Examination for cryptorchidism and, where indicated, evaluation for contiguous gene syndrome features
Maternal serum oestriol history and prenatal genetic testing in at-risk pregnancies
redFlags: Features suggesting a contiguous gene deletion syndrome (e.g. anosmia and hypogonadism, developmental delay)
Failure of scaling to respond to standard care, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: It is a benign, lifelong condition confined largely to the skin in the isolated form, with scaling that persists but is manageable with regular emollient and keratolytic care; prognosis depends on any associated features in patients with larger deletions.
pitfalls: Confusing it with ichthyosis vulgaris, which spares extremities less consistently and is associated with atopy and keratosis pilaris
Overlooking associated cryptorchidism or contiguous gene syndrome features
Failing to recognise the enzyme deficiency implication for atypical labour or low maternal oestriol
Attributing corneal opacities to unrelated ocular disease
management: Regular liberal emollients as the cornerstone of care to soften and reduce retained scale
Keratolytic agents such as urea, lactic acid or other alpha-hydroxy acids to aid desquamation
Topical or, in resistant cases, systemic retinoids under specialist dermatology supervision
Slit-lamp ophthalmology review for corneal opacities, which are typically asymptomatic and need no treatment
Examination for and surgical management of cryptorchidism
Evaluation for a contiguous gene syndrome, such as Kallmann features or learning difficulty, when a larger deletion is present
Genetic counselling with carrier assessment and discussion of prenatal testing in at-risk pregnancies
